He delves further into his memories and recalls one event in the former days of Darlington Hall in which Lord Darlington fired two of his employees for being Jewish. However, Stevens is quick to clarify that his employer was never in the least bit anti-Semitic, but rather that he had made that decision for their own safety, which was threatened by the political climate of the day. Miss Kenton is furious at Lord Darlington’s decision, and she is equally angry at Stevens for his obedient acceptance of it. The Jewish staff are fired and in rage Miss Kenton swears that she will resign, but she does not follow through with this threat. Following this event, Stevens recalls a curious anecdote in which Miss Kenton catches him with a book in his study and, when she asks him what he is reading, he reluctantly reveals that he is reading a sentimental love story, which he claims is an apt genre to improve his spoken command of the English language. Stevens’ journey to Cornwall comes to a halt when his Ford breaks down in a rural village named Moscombe. As his car breaks down at dusk, he decides to spend the evening and night in the modest home of a local couple who offer him dinner and their extra bedroom for his troubles. At this point in Stevens’ recollections, his relationship with Miss Kenton begins to break down. Stevens discontinues their regular evening cup of cocoa when he notes Miss Kenton’s fatigue and lack of interest. She is using her free time to visit someone out of the Hall, a development that Stevens is acutely aware of. At the country cottage in Moscombe, the villagers who are hosting Stevens invite their friends to supper, and they take Stevens to be a refined Lord. Stevens finds himself in a minor argument with one of the villagers, who believes that dignity lies in a person’s ability to engage themselves with important affairs, such as war, money and politics. Stevens disagrees because he sees dignity as the act of loyally serving a just and honourable gentleman such as Lord Darlington, who is well-equipped to further the progress of humanity. A MEETING WITH MISS KENTON Stevens reaches the town of Little Compton in Cornwall, and as he is waiting for the arrival of Miss Kenton, he remembers the night when Mr Cardinal, a journalist and the godson of Lord Darlington, showed up at Darlington Hall to gain information on the international conference that was to take place that night. In this remembered episode, Lord Darlington is to meet with the German Ambassador and Mr Cardinal is frustrated by Lord Darlington’s lenient and accommodating attitude toward the Nazis’ rise to power in Germany. Stevens communicates to Miss Kenton that she must prepare Lord Cardinal’s room, and at this moment she bluntly tells Stevens that the acquaintance she has been seeing in her spare time has asked for her hand in marriage. She notes the unhappiness in Stevens’ face, but he offers no comment concerning her potential marriage, and stoically congratulates her. In Cornwall, Stevens and Miss Kenton are finally reunited. They exchange pleasantries and reminisce about their time working together at Darlington Hall. Miss Kenton assures Stevens that her ongoing marriage, although unstable, is no cause for concern. It is clear that she will not be returning to work at Darlington Hall. Upon saying goodbye, Miss Kenton expresses her anguish at wondering if she could have had a better life, and even mentions that she thinks of a life she may have had with Stevens. Stevens tells her not to lose herself in such foolish ideas, after which the two say goodbye. The next day Stevens is encouraged by a stranger sitting next to him on a bench to try to enjoy the remainder of his life, and following this exchange, he departs back to Darlington Hall. CHARACTER STUDY STEVENS Stevens is the head butler of Darlington Hall and the protagonist-narrator of the novel. In the present moment of the novel, he is a man in the latter half of his life. His employer Mr Farraday remarks to him at the beginning of the novel that he looks like he could “make good use of a break,” indicating to us that he has a somewhat fatigued and elderly appearance (p. 3). Stevens is an exceptionally hard-working individual. He is calculating and deliberate in his actions, and professional to the point where we begin to lose sight of his emotional dimension, as he is so strictly focused only on professional matters. Stevens is polite, courteous, and loyal. On occasion he is unaware of social cues, and the ability to be humorous in the company of others does not come naturally to him. He is a modest figure who enjoys simple pleasures such as the charms a small English village might offer, like a picturesque stone footbridge or a peaceful stream. Ultimately, two of Stevens’ defining characteristics are his traditionalism and his optimism: he is a believer in continual self-improvement and deems it within one’s capability to strive for greatness. This trait is illustrated by the light-hearted ending of the novel in which Stevens looks forward to returning to Darlington Hall to sharpen his bantering skills. MISS KENTON Miss Kenton is the head housekeeper at Darlington Hall and Stevens’ closest acquaintance. As the novel progresses, we see her relationship with Stevens evolve, although it remains professional. Like Stevens, Miss Kenton takes her work very seriously and executes her duties with efficiency and skill, but in contrast to him she is a more lively and colourful character. Interestingly, one of the first memories of Miss Kenton that Stevens recalls tells of how she entered his room with flowers to brighten up his dimly-lit and bare parlour.
